pairs.source_text: Initium mihi operis Servius Galba iterum Titus Vinius consules erunt.
pairs.question: Quibus consulibus initium operis sui Tacitus statuit?
pairs.answer: Servio Galba iterum Tito Vinio consulibus.
pairs.question_en: In whose consulship does Tacitus set the beginning of his work?
pairs.answer_en: In the consulship of Servius Galba (for the second time) and Titus Vinius.
pairs.derivation: The famous opening sentence of the Histories. Anchored to Tacitus's opening + the named consuls of AD 69; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Servius Galba iterum Titus Vinius consules'. Answer recast as ablative absolute (the standard dating idiom). Closed-book: the dating of the Histories' start to Galba's second consulship and Vinius is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: finis Neronis ut laetus primo gaudentium impetu fuerat, ita varios motus animorum non modo in urbe apud patres aut populum aut urbanum militem, sed omnis legiones ducesque conciverat, evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri.
pairs.question: Quod imperii arcanum, finito Nerone, evulgatum esse Tacitus scribit?
pairs.answer: Posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri.
pairs.question_en: What secret of empire does Tacitus write was revealed after Nero's death?
pairs.answer_en: That an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.
pairs.derivation: Tacitus's celebrated 'arcanum imperii'. Anchored to the end of Nero + the secret of empire; supported verbatim by 'evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri'. The fact-seeking form ('what secret') yields the famous maxim as a short clause; indirect statement 'arcanum ... evulgatum esse' governed by scribit. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of the Histories.

pairs.source_text: apud frequentem militum contionem imperatoria brevitate adoptari a se Pisonem exemplo divi Augusti et more militari, quo vir virum legeret, pronuntiat.
pairs.question: Quem Galba sibi successorem in castris adoptavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Galba adopt as his successor in the camp, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Galba + his successor; single named person, supported verbatim by 'adoptari a se Pisonem' (subject Galba). His full name 'Piso Licinianus' is fixed at 1.14 ('Pisonem Licinianum accersiri iubet'). Direct question, indicative adoptavit. Closed-book: Galba's adoption of Piso Licinianus is a stock fact of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: Piso M. Crasso et Scribonia genitus, nobilis utrimque.
pairs.question: Quibus parentibus natus erat Piso Licinianus, quem Galba adoptavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Of what parents was Piso Licinianus, whom Galba adopted, born, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Piso Licinianus (Galba's adopted heir); single named relation, supported verbatim by 'Piso M. Crasso et Scribonia genitus'. Ablative of origin matched in the question ('quibus parentibus natus'). Closed-book named-parentage fact.

pairs.source_text: innixus liberto per Tiberianam domum in Velabrum, inde ad miliarium aureum sub aedem Saturni pergit. ibi tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ac paucitate salutantium trepidum et sellae festinanter impositum strictis mucronibus rapiunt.
pairs.question: A quot speculatoribus Otho ad miliarium aureum primum imperator consalutatus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: By how many speculatores was Otho first hailed as emperor at the golden milestone, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Otho + the golden milestone (the start of his coup); single number, supported verbatim by 'tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ... rapiunt'. Recast as passive (consalutatus est, a + abl.); number kept as 'tres et viginti'. Closed-book: the tiny band of 23 who first hailed Otho is a famous detail.

pairs.source_text: iuxta Curtii lacum trepidatione ferentium Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est.
pairs.question: Iuxta quem locum in foro Galba e sella proiectus et interfectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Beside what place in the forum was Galba thrown from his litter and killed, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Galba's murder; single named place, supported verbatim by 'iuxta Curtii lacum ... Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est' (he is dispatched in the lines following). 'iuxta' + accusative. Closed-book: Galba's death by the Lacus Curtius in the forum is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: hunc exitum habuit Servius Galba, tribus et septuaginta annis quinque principes prospera fortuna emensus et alieno imperio felicior quam suo.
pairs.question: Quot annos natus Servius Galba mortem obiit, ut Tacitus refert?
pairs.question_en: At what age did Servius Galba die, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Galba's death; single number, supported by 'tribus et septuaginta annis ... emensus' (he had traversed 73 years). 'quot annos natus' is the standard age idiom; answer kept as the number 'tres et septuaginta'. Closed-book number fact about Galba.

pairs.source_text: Proxima legionis primae hiberna erant et promptissimus et legatis Fabius Valens. is die postero coloniam Agrippinensem cum equitibus legionis auxiliariorumque ingressus imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit.
pairs.question: Quem Fabius Valens, cum Germaniae legionibus, imperatorem consalutavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Fabius Valens, with the legions of Germany, hail as emperor, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the German legions; single named person, supported verbatim by 'imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit'. Direct question, indicative consalutavit. Closed-book: Vitellius's proclamation by the Rhine armies is the central rival rising of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: sed profusa cupidine et insigni temeritate legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus legatis legionum Vitellius ad imperium nitens praecipue innixus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: On which two legionary legates did Vitellius, striving for power, chiefly rely, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his two legionary legates; two named persons, supported verbatim by 'legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens', who 'instigare Vitellium' (1.52) and are made his two generals at 1.61 ('duos duces ... destinavit'). innitor + ablative; answer in the ablative. Closed-book: Caecina and Valens are Vitellius's famous commanders.

pairs.source_text: Syriam et quattuor legiones obtinebat Licinius Mucianus, vir secundis adversisque iuxta famosus.
pairs.question: Quot legiones in Syria Licinius Mucianus obtinebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: How many legions did Licinius Mucianus hold in Syria, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Licinius Mucianus + Syria; single number, supported verbatim by 'Syriam et quattuor legiones obtinebat Licinius Mucianus'. Direct question, indicative obtinebat. Closed-book number fact about the eastern command in AD 69.

pairs.source_text: bellum Iudaicum Flavius Vespasianus (ducem eum Nero delegerat) tribus legionibus administrabat.
pairs.question: Quot legionibus Flavius Vespasianus bellum Iudaicum administrabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: With how many legions was Flavius Vespasianus conducting the Jewish war, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the Jewish war; single number, supported verbatim by 'bellum Iudaicum Flavius Vespasianus ... tribus legionibus administrabat'. Ablative of means matched in the question. Closed-book: Vespasian's three-legion command in Judaea is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: Aegyptum copiasque, quibus coerceretur, iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum.
pairs.question: Inde a quo principe Aegyptum equites Romani loco regum obtinent, ut Tacitus scribit?
pairs.question_en: From which emperor onward do Roman knights govern Egypt in place of kings, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Egypt + its equestrian government; single named emperor, supported verbatim by 'iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum'. Direct question, indicative obtinent. Closed-book: the rule that Egypt was governed by equestrian prefects (not senators) since Augustus is a well-known institutional fact.

pairs.source_text: quattuor principes ferro interempti: trina bella civilia, plura externa ac plerumque permixta.
pairs.question: Quot principes hoc opere ferro interemptos esse Tacitus initio profitetur?
pairs.question_en: How many emperors does Tacitus declare at the outset were slain by the sword in this work?
pairs.derivation: Programmatic opening of the Histories. Anchored to Tacitus's preface + the emperors of the period it covers; single number, supported verbatim by 'quattuor principes ferro interempti'. Indirect statement 'principes ... interemptos esse' governed by profitetur. Closed-book: the toll of four emperors slain by the sword (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Domitian across the Histories) is a salient programmatic fact.

pairs.source_text: Valenti inferioris exercitus electi cum aquila quintae legionis et cohortibus alisque, ad quadraginta milia armatorum data; triginta milia Caecina e superiore Germania ducebat, quorum robur legio unaetvicensima fuit.
pairs.question: Quot fere milia armatorum Fabio Valenti in Italiam ducenda data sunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: About how many thousand armed men were given to Fabius Valens to lead into Italy, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the Vitellian invasion of Italy; single number, supported verbatim by 'ad quadraginta milia armatorum data' (vs. Caecina's 30,000 in the same sentence). 'fere' mirrors the source's approximative 'ad'; passive 'data sunt' + dative Valenti. Closed-book number fact about the strength of Valens's column.
